# 15.1 Global System Architecture

## Integration Objective

Week 15 begins with architecture, not code volume. Before you attempt final polishing, you need a system map that explains how control enters the program, how objects are created, where collections live, and which methods own each behavior. The objective is to turn the Weeks 10-14 toolset into one predictable runtime.

---

## Architectural Layers

 
 
 
 
 Layer 
 Primary Responsibility 
 Typical Week 15 Implementation 
 
 
 
 
 Controller 
 Read commands, route user intent, and coordinate calls 
 RunMenu() , menu loop, command dispatch methods 
 
 
 Domain model 
 Represent real entities and enforce legal state 
 Student , InventoryItem , TaskRecord , or another custom class 
 
 
 Collection manager 
 Store and iterate over many domain objects 
 List<Student> , List<InventoryItem> , search loops, reports 
 
 
 Validation boundary 
 Reject invalid data before it corrupts the system 
 Validated properties, guarded constructors, input checks before mutation 
 
 
 Reporting layer 
 Produce readable output for operators and grading review 
 Formatted summaries, totals, not-found messages, success confirmation 
 
 
 
 

---

## Reference System Skeleton



The important capstone lesson is not the sample domain. It is the separation of responsibilities. Control stays in the menu loop. State integrity stays in the class. Collection operations stay in methods that receive the list they need.

---

## Integration Sequence

1. Define the domain class first, including the properties and validation rules that make invalid state impossible.
2. Declare the List<T> that owns all runtime records for the application session.
3. Write one method per operator action: add, search, list, update, remove, save, or load.
4. Use return values for lookup and calculation operations so decisions are based on method results instead of duplicated logic.
5. Build the controller loop last, after the underlying methods and class contracts already exist.

---

## Boundary Failures to Eliminate

- Duplicating validation logic in multiple menu branches instead of centralizing it in the class.
- Creating objects directly inside report loops with no constructor contract.
- Storing parallel primitive lists instead of one List<CustomClass> .
- Printing inside every helper method when the method should return data to its caller.
- Allowing a single method to read input, mutate the list, calculate totals, and format reports all at once.

 
 Senior Architect Perspective 
 
 Integration quality is visible in the call graph. A strong capstone project lets you point to the class boundary, the collection owner, and the exact method where each behavior starts and ends. If you cannot describe the path of data through the system, the architecture is still accidental.
 
 

---

# 15.2 Deployment Readiness

Deployment readiness means more than "the code runs on my machine." It means the instructor can execute the project, observe the intended features, test edge conditions, and verify that the architecture matches the written specification. A capstone submission is incomplete until it is testable and reviewable.

---

## Verification Matrix

Build a short matrix before final submission. Every major feature should have one normal execution path and at least one stress case.

 
 
 
 
 Feature 
 Happy-path check 
 Edge-case check 
 Evidence to capture 
 
 
 
 
 Add record 
 Create a valid object and confirm it enters the list 
 Attempt empty text or a negative value and verify rejection 
 Screenshot or console output showing both cases 
 
 
 Search or lookup 
 Find an existing record and print the result 
 Search for a missing key and verify the not-found path 
 Output block with both an existing and missing example 
 
 
 List report 
 Show multiple records with labeled output 
 Run with an empty collection and verify graceful handling 
 Report screenshot with labels visible 
 
 
 Persistence, if used 
 Save data, restart, and reload successfully 
 Test missing file or malformed line handling 
 Cold-start and reload evidence 
 
 
 
 

---

## Submission Package

The Week 15 final delivery should be assembled as an engineering package:

1. The written final reflection submitted on the Week 15 written-final page.
2. Source code for the complete final project.
3. A short run sequence explaining what the instructor should type first.
4. Two to four screenshots or output captures showing major features.
5. Evidence that invalid input is handled without corrupting the system state.
6. Any required data files if the project reads or writes persistent storage.

---

## Recovery Window Triage

If you still have missing work from Weeks 01-14, treat recovery as a controlled backlog, not as a reason to postpone the capstone baseline.

1. Stabilize the final project architecture first.
2. Complete the highest-value missing recovery items during the Week 15 window.
3. Assume every recovered assignment or quiz is capped at 70%.
4. Do not let recovery work consume the final testing pass for the capstone submission.

---

## Deployment Checklist

- Run the project from a clean start without editing code during the demonstration.
- Confirm at least one custom class, one encapsulated property boundary, one List<T> workflow, and multiple named methods are visible in the final code.
- Remove placeholder output and ambiguous prompts.
- Verify that the instructor can reach the major features in under five minutes.
- Confirm the written final and final project were both submitted, and both scores resolve to the Final category.
